content: 1. Patients who transfer into a facility are recorded in the ART register under their original ART initiation cohort (month/year). A line is drawn to distinguish them from those who started ART at the receiving facility, and a note indicating transfer in is added in the margin. These individuals are not included in the cumulative count of patients who have ever started ART at the receiving facility, as they were already recorded as having started ART at another site. 2. A transfer involving an individual who has received ART from external sources or within the system but lacks records of their ART regimen or start date is classified as Earlier ARVs not transfer in. This person is considered newly enrolled in HIV care. 3. A transfer involving an individual with records who has not yet started ART and moves between facilities or from a community service delivery organization to a health facility is classified as Transfer in: naive. This individual will have an existing enrolled in HIV care date, and the HIV care transfer in from box will be checked and completed. 4. A transfer involving an individual without records who has not yet started ART and moves between facilities or from a community service delivery organization to a health facility is classified as newly enrolled in HIV care having no prior ARVs. This individual may be double-counted as newly enrolled in HIV care. These categories apply whether the patient is transferring between HIV services at different health facilities or from MNCH or TB services into HIV services, or vice versa. 5. The term START refers to the date a patient begins their first ART regimen in the system or the date they started ART under another program or practitioner, if known. For example, if a patient starts ART at Clinic A and later transfers to Clinic B, Clinic A records the start date, and Clinic B copies this date into their records. 6. The term STOP refers to the date a patient intentionally discontinues an ART regimen, typically in consultation with the clinical team. This includes patients who are no longer on ART but remain in care. 7. The term RESTART refers to the date a patient resumes ART after previously stopping, regardless of the regimen. Operationally, patients restarting ART after an interruption of three months or more are considered to be restarting treatment. 8. Lost to Follow-Up (LTFU) includes patients who have not been seen at the facility or community service delivery site for 28 days or more since their last missed appointment, including missed ARV refills. A one-month grace period is allowed before concluding that a patient is LTFU. Facilities should make every effort to contact patients as soon as they miss an appointment, rather than waiting for the 28-day period. 9. The term TRANSFER OUT refers to the date a person receiving ART at one facility or community ART site transfers out to another site. 10. The term DEAD refers to a person who has died at any time after being enrolled in HIV care. 11. SUBSTITUTE refers to the replacement of ARV drugs within the same line of treatment (first-, second-, or third-line), with the date and reason documented. 12. SWITCH refers to a change from one line of treatment to another (e.g., first-line to second-line), with the date and reason documented. 13. The Cumulative Ever-Started on ART count includes the number of people who have ever started ART as new at the facility. It excludes those who transferred in but includes those who later transferred out, died, were LTFU, or stopped treatment. 14. People Living with HIV on ART refers to a cross-sectional count of individuals currently on ART at a given site, including those who transferred in. This informs the calculation of attrition during the reporting period. 15. A Cohort refers to a group of people living with HIV who start ART in a given month (or quarter) and year, whose status is followed over time using the ART register. 16. The Net Current Cohort includes people living with HIV in each cohort for whom the facility is currently responsible. This includes those who started ART at the facility in a given month/quarter and year, minus those who transferred out, plus those who transferred in. 17. Health workers should create an HIV treatment and care patient card or electronic medical record (EMR) for every person confirmed HIV-positive, regardless of the entry point (e.g., HIV, MNCH, or TB services). ART registers or electronic equivalents should be maintained at all sites providing ART. 18. Community ART providers engaged in ART delivery should routinely monitor and report on a minimum key set of data in a standardized manner. 19. The HIV patient monitoring system is designed to capture and retain data on all individuals with a confirmed HIV diagnosis and follow them through the cascade of HIV care services, from diagnosis and ART initiation to sustained viral suppression. 20. The ART register contains key information from the HIV patient card, is organized by the month and year of ART initiation, and records follow-up data, including CD4 count, viral load, and enrollment in differentiated service delivery (DSD) models. It is used to aggregate data into ART cohort and cross-sectional reports. 21. WHO recommends maintaining ART registers in paper or electronic form wherever people living with HIV receive treatment. This facilitates data reconciliation for TB-HIV and HIV/MNCH indicators and allows for longitudinal follow-up of cohorts.
